title: A Prom for the Locker
premise: August Thornbury, the only out kid in the dying town of Locker, Montana, has learned to survive by being fine — until the school's legendary ghost begins leaving him notes written in ink that shouldn't exist, each one naming a wrong done decades ago. The notes belong to Delia Marsh, a girl erased from the town's history in 1971, and August, along with his prickly best friend Priya and the ghost's last living relative, must uncover what Locker buried: a theft of land, a life, and a name. Telling the truth means exposing the founding family — the Thornburys, August's own inheritance — and losing the one friendship he can't afford to lose. In the end, August chooses justice over comfort, gives Delia's stolen inheritance back to her surviving kin, and discovers that found family isn't the one that claims you but the ones who stay while you burn your name down and build a truer one.
about_author: Astrid Vasquez grew up in a town so small her graduating class held four people, three of them cousins. She writes stories about queer kids in places that would rather forget them, and she has never once been fine, obviously.

chapters.title: Everything Is Fine, Obviously
chapters.summary: August's POV. We meet August navigating Locker High's halls, his carefully managed 'fine' persona, his widowed grandmother's silence about the family past, and Priya — his only friend, whose loyalty has cracks. Beat: loneliness disguised as control.

chapters.title: The First Note
chapters.summary: August's POV. A note appears inside his locker addressed to him by name: 'You're not the only one who was ever alone in here. — D.' The ink is wet, though the locker's been sealed overnight. Beat: wonder piercing routine.

chapters.title: Local Legend, Poorly Researched
chapters.summary: August's POV. He digs into the school ghost story — 'the Marsh Girl,' who supposedly haunts the east stairwell — and finds the yearbooks from 1971 have a page torn out. Priya catches him snooping and warns him off. Beat: first fracture.

chapters.title: Impossible Ink
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya tests the ink in chemistry class; it matches nothing, contains compounds decades out of use. She's furious at being pulled in — and more furious at how much she wants in. Beat: reluctant curiosity.

chapters.title: The Second Note
chapters.summary: August's POV. A second note names a person: 'Ask your grandmother about the Marsh orchard.' August realizes the ghost knows his family. His grandmother goes white and orders him to drop it. Beat: dread replacing wonder.

chapters.title: Orchard Road
chapters.summary: August's POV. August bikes out to the overgrown Marsh orchard at the town's edge and finds fresh-cut flowers on an unmarked grave — someone is still tending it. He hides and watches an old man leave. Beat: the past is alive.

chapters.title: Wes Marsh
chapters.summary: August's POV. August tracks down Wes Marsh, Delia's younger brother, now in his sixties, who tends the grave but won't speak. 'The Thornburys bought this town with something that wasn't theirs,' is all he says. Beat: the enemy has August's own name.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Buried
chapters.summary: August's POV. August confronts his grandmother with the notes. She reveals a fragment: 1971, a fire, a girl blamed for it, and a deed signed by August's late grandfather that 'wasn't clean.' Beat: inheritance curdles into shame.

chapters.title: Priya's Price
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya, whose family depends on Thornbury-owned packing plant jobs, begs August to stop — if the Thornburys fall, her father falls. She calls his crusade selfish. Beat: friendship versus justice, stated outright.

chapters.title: The Third Note
chapters.summary: August's POV. The note is a map of the school's east stairwell and one word: 'BEHIND.' August and Priya, still barely speaking, pry loose a brick and find Delia's journal, half-burned. Beat: alliance rekindled by evidence.

chapters.title: Delia's Voice
chapters.summary: August's POV. The journal: Delia Marsh was brilliant, queer, and in love with a Thornbury — August's grandfather's younger brother. The fire wasn't hers; she was blamed to bury what she knew about the forged deed. Beat: the ghost becomes a person.

chapters.title: She's Not Dead
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya realizes the notes aren't from a ghost: the ink compounds match a discontinued 1970s formulation — someone alive is writing them. The old man at the grave? No — Wes Marsh is dying and couldn't have. There's someone else. Beat: mystery pivots.

chapters.title: The Substitute
chapters.summary: August's POV. The new long-term substitute teacher, Ms. Vale, has Delia's handwriting. August tests her gently; she denies everything, but her classroom copy of the 1971 yearbook has the torn page restored. Beat: the ghost has a face.

chapters.title: Ms. Vale's Confession
chapters.summary: Ms. Vale's POV. Delia Marsh never died in the fire — she was run out of town, pregnant, and erased. Vale is her daughter, raised on her mother's unfinished fight, finishing it now that Delia is fading in a hospice two states away. Beat: grief and purpose entwined.

chapters.title: The Deed
chapters.summary: August's POV. The journal plus the restored yearbook page plus grandmother's fragment reconstruct the forgery: August's grandfather stole the Marsh orchard and water rights, the town's economic spine. Proof exists in the county records vault. Beat: the plan forms.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred Witnesses
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya flips: if the truth comes out right — with restitution, not ruin — her father's job survives under new ownership. She starts building the townside case: old ledgers, elderly witnesses, the packing plant's original charter. Beat: Priya becomes the strategist.

chapters.title: The Thornbury Name
chapters.summary: August's POV. Grandmother, cornered by the full evidence, makes her choice: she hands August her late husband's hidden copy of the real deed — she's known for fifty years and stayed silent. 'I was a coward,' she says. 'Don't be me.' Beat: the older generation's reckoning.

chapters.title: Running Out of Time
chapters.summary: August's POV. The county records vault is scheduled for digitization and purge — the physical originals will be destroyed in ten days. Meanwhile Ms. Vale is dismissed when a school board member (a Thornbury cousin) connects her to Delia. Beat: clock starts, stakes spike.

chapters.title: The Vault
chapters.summary: August, Priya, and Ms. Vale's POV alternating. They legally request the originals; the board stalls; Priya discovers a public-records statute that forces release. A tense records-room standoff with the board chair ends with the certified copies in hand. Beat: victory by procedure, not luck.

chapters.title: Prom
chapters.summary: August's POV. The board threatens expulsion and the town splits; at prom — which August almost skips — he walks in with Priya and Ms. Vale, and half the school, led by kids whose families were also cheated, stands with him. Beat: public truth-telling as celebration.

chapters.title: Delia Marsh, In Full
chapters.summary: August's POV. At the hospice, August reads Delia her own restored name back into the record: the deed returned, the orchard deeded to Wes and Delia's heirs, her yearbook page reprinted in the local paper. Delia, barely conscious, writes one last note in her impossible ink: 'Thank you for finding me.' Beat: restitution, grief, grace.

chapters.title: A Prom for the Locker
chapters.summary: August's POV, months later. The school is renamed Marsh Community High; the first spring festival is held in the orchard. Grandmother and Wes Marsh sit together at the same table. August is still the only out kid in a town of nine hundred — and for the first time, that's not the same as being alone. Beat: found family, earned and kept.
